Gastrointestinal Disorders

Disorders Presenting Primarily With Diarrhea

Diarrhea chapters are hydration and danger-pattern chapters. Most patients have self-limited gastroenteritis, but the ED misses are dysentery, dehydration, sepsis, C. difficile, toxic megacolon, obstruction, ischemia, and IBD complications.

Board trap: Do not give reflex loperamide or reflex antibiotics before deciding whether the patient has invasive diarrhea, Shiga toxin risk, C. difficile, ileus, or toxic megacolon.

GENERAL ASSESSMENT OF PATIENTS WITH DIARRHEA

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Acute diarrhea is increased stool water content and frequency. Most ED cases are viral, but bacteria, parasites, medications, diet products, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemia, endocrine disease, and immunocompromise change the risk. Hydration status and toxicity drive urgency before the organism is known.

Rosen source

Table 80.1

Gastroenteritis epidemiologic factors.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen Ch.80 gives organism-specific diagnosis, clinical features, and empiric-treatment detail; Tintinalli Ch.73 organizes the ED approach around traveler diarrhea, C. difficile, IBD/Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, disposition, and toxic megacolon.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Diarrhea occurs through secretory, osmotic, inflammatory, and motility mechanisms. Preformed toxins cause abrupt vomiting/diarrhea; invasive organisms cause fever, tenesmus, abdominal pain, and blood; parasites and postinfectious conditions cause persistent symptoms.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Assess stool frequency, blood, mucus, fever, abdominal tenderness, tenesmus, travel, camping, seafood, antibiotics, hospitalization, sick contacts, outbreak, sexual exposures, immune status, and volume depletion. Severe abdominal pain or peritoneal findings are not simple gastroenteritis until proven otherwise.

DIAGNOSTIC STOOL EVALUATION

Stool testing is not routine for mild illness. Test when there is dysentery, fever, severe disease, immunocompromise, outbreak/public-health concern, persistent diarrhea, recent antibiotics, or suspected C. difficile/parasites. PCR panels are fast but must be interpreted with the clinical syndrome.

TREATMENT

Core care is oral or IV rehydration, electrolyte correction, antiemetics when needed, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics, and safe use of antimotility agents. Oral rehydration works for mild to moderate dehydration; shock or severe dehydration needs IV crystalloid.

ACUTE INFECTIOUS AND TRAVELER'S DIARRHEA

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Traveler diarrhea risk follows destination, food/water exposure, season, host factors, and sanitation. ETEC is common, while Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, parasites, and viruses vary by region and exposure.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Watery diarrhea without fever is often viral or toxigenic. Fever, bloody stool, tenesmus, severe cramps, and systemic toxicity suggest invasive bacterial disease. Persistent watery diarrhea after travel raises Giardia, Cyclospora, Cryptosporidium, or Entamoeba depending on exposure.

TREATMENT

Use rehydration first. Empiric antibiotics shorten selected bacterial/traveler diarrhea but are avoided for suspected Shiga toxin E. coli. Azithromycin is favored in many travel scenarios, especially where fluoroquinolone resistance is likely; rifaximin is only for noninvasive diarrhea.

Tintinalli source

Table 73-2

Antimicrobial recommendations for infectious pathogens in adults.

DISPOSITION

Discharge is reasonable for improving, hydrated, nontoxic patients who can drink and return if worse. Admit for severe dehydration, shock, electrolyte derangement, severe abdominal pain, immunocompromise, inability to tolerate PO, or unreliable follow-up.

CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE-ASSOCIATED DIARRHEA AND COLITIS

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

C. difficile ranges from mild diarrhea to fulminant pseudomembranous colitis. Antibiotic exposure and healthcare contact are classic, but community disease occurs. Elderly, immunocompromised, hospitalized, and recently antibiotic-treated patients are high risk.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt colonic flora; toxin-producing C. difficile then causes mucosal inflammation and systemic toxicity. Ileus can hide diarrhea in fulminant disease.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Symptoms usually occur during antibiotics or within weeks after stopping. Watery diarrhea, cramps, fever, leukocytosis, dehydration, ileus, shock, and toxic megacolon form the severity spectrum.

DIAGNOSIS

Test diarrheal stool using local toxin/PCR algorithms; do not test formed stool. Severe disease requires labs for WBC, creatinine, electrolytes, lactate, and imaging when ileus, megacolon, perforation, or alternate diagnosis is suspected.

TREATMENT

Stop inciting antibiotics when possible, provide fluids/electrolytes, isolate/contact precautions, and use oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin by severity. Fulminant disease needs urgent GI/surgery involvement and often combined therapy.

Tintinalli source

Table 73-3

Treatment of Clostridium difficile infection by severity.

DISPOSITION

Hospitalize severe dehydration, clinical toxicity, persistent symptoms despite therapy, recurrent high-risk disease, or concern for toxic megacolon, ileus, or perforation. Do not discharge a toxic C. difficile patient with only oral hydration advice.

INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE/ILEITIS/COLITIS/CROHN'S DISEASE

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Crohn disease can involve any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, often with transmural inflammation and skip lesions. ED presentations include flare, infection superimposed on IBD, obstruction, abscess, fistula, bleeding, malnutrition, and medication complications.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Transmural granulomatous inflammation produces ulceration, strictures, fistulas, and abscesses. Active disease and steroid/biologic exposure change infection risk and blunt classic signs.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, fever, anorexia, perianal disease, and extraintestinal symptoms are common. Worsening pain pattern in known Crohn disease should trigger abscess, obstruction, or fistula thinking.

Tintinalli source

Table 73-4

Common extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease.

DIAGNOSIS

Evaluate for dehydration, anemia, inflammation, infection, electrolyte derangement, obstruction, abscess, and medication effects. CT with contrast is common for complications; MRI is useful for fistula/perianal disease when available.

TREATMENT

Resuscitate, correct electrolytes, treat infection/abscess, consult GI/surgery for complications, and avoid reflex antidiarrheals in toxic patients. Steroids or biologics depend on disease severity and infection exclusion.

Tintinalli source

Table 73-5

Treatment of fulminant colitis.

DISEASE COMPLICATIONS

Abscess, fissure, fistula, stricture, obstruction, perforation, malnutrition, nephrolithiasis, hepatobiliary disease, ocular disease, arthritis, and skin disease can dominate the ED presentation.

DISPOSITION

Admit toxic patients, severe dehydration, obstruction, abscess, peritonitis, GI bleeding, severe flare, or uncertain diagnosis. Stable mild flares with reliable follow-up may discharge after discussion with the treating clinician.

ULCERATIVE COLITIS

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Ulcerative colitis is continuous mucosal disease beginning in the rectum and extending proximally. ED visits occur for flare, bleeding, dehydration, infection, medication complications, and toxic megacolon.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Mucosal inflammation causes bloody diarrhea, urgency, tenesmus, and systemic inflammation. Severe colitis can paralyze the colon and lead to toxic dilation.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Bloody stool, cramps, urgency, fever, tachycardia, dehydration, and anemia define severity. Antidiarrheals are dangerous if toxic megacolon is possible.

DIAGNOSIS

Check CBC, electrolytes, renal function, inflammatory markers when useful, stool testing for infection including C. difficile, and abdominal imaging when severe colitis, distention, peritonitis, or megacolon is suspected.

TREATMENT

Treat dehydration and electrolyte loss, stop antidiarrheals in severe disease, consult GI, use steroids/biologics by severity and specialist input, and involve surgery for fulminant colitis or megacolon.

DISEASE COMPLICATIONS

Toxic megacolon causes colonic dilation, systemic toxicity, leukocytosis, anemia, electrolyte derangement, and risk of perforation. The Tintinalli figure shows the radiographic pattern to recognize quickly.

Tintinalli source

Figure 73-1

Abdominal distention due to toxic megacolon.

DISPOSITION

Admit fulminant attacks, suspected toxic megacolon, severe hemorrhage, perforation, severe dehydration, renal injury, or uncontrolled symptoms. Mild to moderate stable patients can discharge only with close GI follow-up and return precautions.
